name: Scene Graph Consistency
description: Builds and validates temporal scene graphs to detect object appearance/disappearance anomalies in AI-generated video.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or manipulated video by building temporal scene graphs and checking for physically impossible object relationship changes:

1. **Scene Graph Construction**: For each frame, the method builds a scene graph — a structured representation where nodes are detected objects (people, vehicles, furniture, etc.) and edges represent spatial relationships between them (on top of, next to, behind, inside, holding, etc.). Object detection uses Faster R-CNN or DETR, and relationship classification uses a visual relationship detection network (VTransE or Neural Motifs). Each node stores: object category, bounding box, appearance feature vector (2048-d ResNet), and identity embedding for re-identification. Each edge stores: relationship type, spatial configuration (above, left-of, occluding), and distance estimate. A typical frame produces 10–50 nodes and 20–200 edges.

2. **Temporal Graph Alignment**: Scene graphs from consecutive frames are aligned to track objects and relationships over time. Object correspondences are established using: (a) IoU (intersection-over-union) overlap > 0.5 with the previous frame, (b) appearance similarity — cosine similarity > 0.8 between feature vectors, (c) motion prediction — Kalman filter predicts expected position. The aligned temporal graph tracks how each object and each relationship evolves over time. Object identity is maintained through an embedding-based tracker (DeepSORT) to handle occlusion and re-appearance.

3. **Physical Plausibility Validation**: The method checks the temporal scene graph for physically impossible transitions: (a) object permanence violations — an object disappears without leaving the frame or being occluded (AI generators sometimes 'forget' objects), (b) teleportation — an object's position changes by more than physically possible given frame rate (e.g., > 100 pixels/frame for a walking person at 30 fps), (c) relationship violations — 'on top of' transitions to 'inside' without any physical mechanism, (d) count inconsistencies — the number of objects of a given class changes without objects entering or exiting the frame. Each violation is scored by severity, and the accumulated score indicates generation probability.

4. **Semantic Consistency Checking**: Beyond spatial relationships, the method validates semantic coherence over time: (a) object attributes should change gradually — a red car should not become blue between frames, (b) functional relationships should persist — a person sitting on a chair should continue that relationship until a visible action changes it, (c) relative depth ordering should remain consistent unless there is a clear motion event, (d) scene-level statistics — the total number of people in a crowd should not fluctuate randomly. AI-generated long-form video often fails semantic consistency because autoregressive generation accumulates errors, and different conditioning windows produce incompatible scene states.
parameters:
Object detection: Faster R-CNN / DETR
Relationship detection: Neural Motifs / VTransE
Appearance features: ResNet-50, 2048-d
Tracking: DeepSORT with Kalman filter
IoU correspondence threshold: > 0.5
Appearance similarity threshold: > 0.8
Teleportation threshold: > 100 pixels/frame (person)
Object permanence: minimum 5 frames after disappearance
Attribute change threshold: color distance < 15 in L*a*b*
Analysis window: 90 frames (3 seconds at 30fps)
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated video via scene graph consistency. Object permanence violation detection achieves AUC of 0.87. Semantic consistency provides F1-score of 0.84. Performance improves with longer video sequences (> 5 seconds) where accumulation errors become more apparent.
source: Xu, D. et al. (2017). Scene Graph Generation by Iterative Message Passing. CVPR, 5410–5419.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated long-form video through object relationship inconsistencies. Forensic analysis of video timeline integrity. Validating temporal coherence of synthetic environments. Identifying frame insertion or deletion in surveillance footage.
strengths:
• Captures high-level semantic inconsistencies missed by pixel-level methods
• Object permanence is a strong physical constraint
• Relationship tracking provides rich multi-signal analysis
• Performance improves with video length — more opportunities to catch errors
• Works independently of visual quality or resolution
limitations:
• Requires accurate object detection and relationship classification
• Short clips (< 2 seconds) provide insufficient temporal signal
• Simple scenes with few objects produce sparse graphs
• Computational cost scales with number of objects per frame
• Some AI generators with explicit object tracking may maintain consistency
